fetched_contents.text: Histology, Periodontium - StatPearls Introduction The periodontium is a connective tissue consisting of four components: cementum, the periodontal ligament (PDL), alveolar bone, and gingival tissue (see Image. Periodontium Anatomy).[1] This topic details the histological and embryological structure and origin of this tissue, as well as the function, clinical significance, and pathophysiology of some of the periodontal diseases. Structure Embryologically, PDL, cementum, and alveolar bone development are accompanied by the formation of the root of the tooth and its eruption.[2] However, the gingival component of the periodontium is derived from the ectoderm of the pharyngeal arches. It contains keratinized stratified squamous epithelium on its masticatory surface and non-keratinized on its crevicular and junctional surface.[1] As mentioned, PDL, cementum, and alveolar bone are derived from the dental sac's neuro-mesenchymal stem cells.[3] To better understand the gingival epithelium, it can be studied in three different sections: the oral epithelium, sulcular epithelium, and junctional epithelium, which is the closest to the tooth surface and attaches to it with hemidesmosomes. Histologically, cementum is comprised of two parts: cellular and acellular. The gingival epithelium is composed of stratified squamous epithelium. Function The periodontium functions include supporting the tooth, protecting it against oral microflora, and making the attachment of the tooth to the bone possible.[1] To understand the function of the periodontium even further, we can look at its components function individually. The PDL is a connective tissue that consists mostly of type I collagen bands and fibroblasts. Using collagen bands, PDL connects the tooth's cementum to the gingivae in the alveolar socket. On the other hand, fibroblasts have a role in forming and repairing the alveolar bone and cementum.[4] Besides attaching the tooth roots to the bone and gingival tissue, PDL is also involved in proprioception by relaying information to the somatosensory cortex. This is important for avoiding occlusal forces during mastication and speech.[5] Cementum is the mineralized tissue covering the dentin surfaces and is known to be the attachment site for PDL. Tissue Preparation Various processing techniques have been suggested and studied in the literature, exploring different fixing and demineralizing solutions for tooth and periodontium. In light microscopy analysis done on histological processing of teeth and periodontium, it was demonstrated that 10% buffered neutral formalin was used as a fixative solution and 10% pH 7.3 EDTA, as a demineralizing solution, has shown satisfactory results. Paraffin-embedded sections of the sample are obtained to obtain morphometric and morphological satisfaction, each with a thickness of 6 μm. These slides were then stained with hematoxylin and eosin. This routine protocol is also beneficial since it allows serial sectioning for more specific techniques. For instance, this routine protocol can use techniques such as histochemical and immunohistochemical analyses that are more fitting for evaluating cellular components and the extracellular matrix of the periodontium.[6] The biologically oriented preparation technique is a reliable alternative to conventional horizontal finish lines.[7] In a cross-sectional study conducted in Turkey by Alkan et al, the effects of antibiotic therapy in oral histology were studied. The results showed that in healthy participants in oral histology trials, a minimum of 3 months should pass after the final amoxicillin dose to avoid the negative effect of gingival tissue smear samples.[8] Pathophysiology Understanding the structure and histology of the periodontium is clinically significant to the discussion of wound healing, drugs and environmental factors affecting it, periodontal diseases, and overall health risk factors. Lamina propria of gingiva regenerates more readily due to fiber differentiation after wounding, compared to the alveolar bone, which relies on osteocyte, bone marrow cells, endosteum cells, and osteogenic cells of periosteum, which occupy different compartments.[1] Histopathology of periodontal diseases is described in 4 stages: 1. Initially, the gingival crevicular fluid amount is increased due to vascular changes in response to the initial insult. At this benign stage, polymorphonuclear neutrophils are attracted to the lesion site, and T lymphocytes are responsible for fibroblasts. 2. The early lesion is characterized by redness. At this stage, PMNs clear and breakdown the collagen fibers, which increases the previously made space for infiltrates. 3. At this stage, the established lesion is dominated by B cells and leukocyte aggregation. This initiates the lesion side transformation by changing the junctional and sulcular epithelium into an extremely vulnerable epithelium called the pocket epithelium. This is apparent as bleeding upon gentle gingival manipulation. 4. An advanced lesion characterized as loss of gingival fibers and alveolar bone is caused by the migration of biofilm into the pocket and creating an environment for anaerobic bacterias' proliferation.[9] * Gingivitis is an initial response to combat the first insult to the periodontium. As the name suggests, it is an inflammation of the gingiva, a component of the periodontium resulting from the accumulation of microbial plaque near the gingival sulcus. Gingivitis has a delayed appearance in children with a predominance of T lymphocyte infiltrates.[10] Most cases are transient, non-progressive, and reversible. However, it can progress to Periodontitis. * Periodontitis is the inflammation of the periodontium, which extends to the jawbone and is irreversible (see Image. Periodontitis). Published in final edited form as: Periodontol 2000. 2014 Feb;64(1):57–80. doi: 10.1111/prd.12002 ---------------------------------------- Inflammation is the physiological response to a variety of injuries or insults, including heat, chemical agents or bacterial infection. In the acute phase of inflammation, the response is rapid and of short duration. If the insult or injury is not resolved, the response becomes chronic, which can be considered as nonphysiologic or pathologic. When inflammation becomes chronic, the adaptive immune response is activated with involvement of the cellular and non-cellular mechanisms of acquired immunity. Immune mechanisms play further roles in the resolution of inflammation and in the healing process, including the repair and the regeneration of lost or damaged tissues. Thus, innate (inflammatory) immunity and acquired immunity must be coordinated to return the injured tissue to homeostasis (85). The etiology of periodontal diseases is bacteria. The human oral cavity harbors a substantial and continuously evolving load of microbial species. The ecological interactions between the host and microbes determine the severity of the disease. Unlike many infectious diseases, periodontal diseases appear to be infections mediated by the overgrowth of commensal organisms, rather than by the acquisition of an exogenous pathogen. As microorganisms evolve more rapidly than their mammalian hosts, immune mechanisms that determine the ecological balance of commensal organisms also need to change to preserve homeostasis (65). Knowledge of how immune mechanisms and inflammatory responses are regulated is critical for understanding the pathogenesis of complex diseases, such as periodontitis. The pathogenesis of periodontal diseases is mediated by the inflammatory response to bacteria in the dental biofilm (Fig. 1). However, identification of the true ‘pathogens’ in periodontitis has been elusive. There is evidence that specific microbes are associated with the progressive forms of the disease; however, the presence of these microorganisms in individuals with no evidence of disease progression suggests that the disease is the net effect of the immune response and the inflammatory processes, not the mere presence of the bacteria. Regulation of immune–inflammatory mechanisms governs patient susceptibility and is modified by environmental factors (219, 220, 241). This review will address the pathways of inflammation in periodontal diseases by focusing on immunologic mechanisms to elucidate sites of regulation. Clinical features of the periodontal diseases are beyond the scope of this work but are within the context of the pathogenic mechanisms. Possible clinical outcomes will be discussed in relation to the inflammatory–immunologic changes throughout the disease process. Periodontal diseases: what do we know? There are two common diseases affecting the periodontium. The first is gingivitis, which is defined as inflammation of the gingiva in which the connective tissue attachment to the tooth remains at its original level. The disease is limited to the soft-tissue compartment of the gingival epithelium and connective tissue (12). The second is periodontitis, which is an inflammation of the supporting tissues of the teeth with progressive attachment loss and bone destruction (55). Both diseases and their symptoms are very common in populations worldwide. In the USA, adolescents have gingivitis and signs of gingival bleeding, whereas 54% of the adult population in the USA exhibits gingival bleeding (99). Thirty-seven per cent of the adult population in the USA suffers from severe periodontitis (160). In both cases, the disease is associated with the accumulation of bacteria at the dento–gingival margin, while the causal relationship of specific organisms is not fully clear. The host responds to microbial challenge by generating an inflammatory cell infiltrate in the tissue subjacent to the periodontal pocket (186). The initial inflammation in the periodontal tissues should be considered a physiologic defense mechanism against the microbial challenge, rather than pathology. The clinical findings of the disease at this stage include supragingival and subgingival plaque formation, which are usually accompanied by calculus formation and gingival inflammation (154). If plaque is removed, there is resolution with return to homeostasis; if the lesion persists, it becomes pathology. For convenience, we will use the well-known stages of gingivitis and periodontitis, described by Page & Schroeder, in 1976 (186), for descriptive purposes: the initial lesion; the early lesion; the established lesion; and the advanced lesion. The advanced lesion is also called the destructive phase, because it represents the transition from gingivitis to periodontitis. What makes inflammation and immunologic events underlying periodontal diseases confusing is that the immunologic events overlap in different phases of disease. It should be emphasized that division of the immune response into various systems, such as innate immunity and adaptive immunity, is a rather arbitrary distinction imposed by immunologists (12). Although it is easier to describe the inflammation in compartments, the mechanisms involved in inflammation, resolution and healing include all components of the immune system that interact cooperatively to protect the periodontium (266). fetched_contents.text: Periodontal Disease - StatPearls Continuing Education Activity Periodontal disease encompasses inflammatory conditions affecting the periodontium—the gingiva, periodontal ligament, cementum, and alveolar bone. The condition typically begins as gingivitis, a reversible inflammation caused by plaque accumulation that affects up to 90% of the population. Without intervention, gingivitis can progress to periodontitis, which is a chronic, destructive, and irreversible condition characterized by loss of attachment, alveolar bone resorption, and eventual tooth loss. This disease affects 90% of people worldwide and leads to inflammatory disorders of the periodontal tissue and even other organs.1 On the basis of findings from the Global Burden of Disease Study 2019, there has been a global escalation in the age-standardised rates of periodontitis prevalence, incidence, and disability-adjusted life years from 1990 to 2019.2 Consequently, researchers are dedicated to studying treatments for periodontal disease. Over the past few decades, several traditional treatments, such as scaling and root planning have been commonly used and have achieved significant clinical effects. Such treatments delay the process of inflammation by removing plaque and calculus but are unable to restore the original connective tissue and reconstruct the intricate organisation of the periodontal complex (PDL, cementum, and alveolar bone).3 Thus, functional restoration of the multitissue periodontal complex is needed. In this process, one of the key steps is to attach PDL to the mineralisation layer formed on the surface of the bone and tooth root.4 Some regeneration surgeries, such as guided tissue regeneration (GTR) and bone grafting, are effective only for bone regeneration but have yielded limited success in regenerating the structural and functional aspects of cementum, which reminds us to pay more attention to cementum regeneration. The cementum is an avascular mineralisation structure that connects teeth to alveolar bone through PDL fibres.5 The most important function of the cementum is to serve as an anchor point for the main PDL fibres on the surface of the tooth root. Such anchoring helps maintain the occlusal relationship and supports the teeth through a markedly dynamic response.6 The regeneration of cementum is considered essential for fostering the attachment of new fibrous tissues, maintaining the integrity of the PDL, and preventing the occurrence of tooth ankylosis.4 The stability of teeth and their protection against resorption depend heavily on the integrity of the cementum. Periodontal inflammation damages the cells and the cementum on the tooth root, leading to the growth of the epithelium and the formation of a crevice where bacteria accumulate. The loss of cementum disrupts the microbial barrier and leads to the deterioration of periodontitis.7 Research indicates that individuals with cementum deficiency or abnormalities are prone to early-onset periodontitis, which results in abnormal attachment and increases the vulnerability of teeth to periodontal pathogens.8 Therefore, the regeneration of cementum, especially when it incorporates functional fibres, is vital for the development of periodontal tissue and is an important step in periodontal regeneration.4,9 However, owing to the complex structure of cementum, the understanding of how it regenerates still lags well behind the knowledge regarding other periodontal tissue.6,10 The cementogenic procedure for PDL attachments remains a challenge in periodontal regeneration.11 Considering that cementum generation is important for its support, protection, and fixation effects on teeth and is crucial for preserving the PDL and regenerating periodontal tissue, we summarise the current basic research and clinical technologies related to cementum regeneration. It is anticipated that periodontal tissue regenerative medicine will ultimately benefit the clinical treatment of periodontitis. Classification and development of cementum Classification of cementum Histologically, cementum can be categorised into cellular cementum and acellular cementum on the basis of whether it contains cementocytes.12 There are 2 varieties of collagen fibres in the cementum. Extrinsic fibres, namely, perforating fibres or Sharpey's fibres, are partly generated by PDL fibroblasts and partly by cementoblasts, serving a crucial function in anchoring the cementum to the alveolar bone. Thus, the formation of Sharpey's fibres facilitates recovery of the functional regeneration of cementum. Intrinsic fibres are inherent fibres created by cementoblasts.13 On the basis of the distribution of the cementocytes and the origin of the collagen fibres, cementum can be classified into 5 detailed categories: acellular afibrillar cementum (AAC), acellular extrinsic fibre cementum (AEFC), cellular intrinsic fibre cementum (CIFC), acellular intrinsic fibre cementum (AIFC) and cellular mixed stratified cementum (CMSC) (Figure 1). Among these types, AEFC and CMSC are embedded with abundant Sharpey's fibres,5,14 which play essential roles in cementum regeneration. The AEFC is located at the cervical root surface. It contains no cells and is composed of densely arranged collagen fibre bundles (also referred to as Sharpey's fibres, which are perpendicular to the root surface). CMSC is composed of a mixture of multiple areas of AEFC and CIFC that cover the interradicular and apical areas of roots.13,14 In summary, differentiation into various types of cementum is highly important for its generation. Periodontal damage disrupts tooth support and infection control by breaking down the structural and defensive roles of the periodontium, as shown in the provided evidence. Attachment loss and bone resorption weaken tooth stability because periodontitis causes progressive destruction of the periodontal tissues, with loss of attachment, alveolar bone resorption, and eventual tooth loss [N4-F3]. Clinical signs such as gingival bleeding, periodontal pocketing, radiographic bone loss, and tooth mobility are used for diagnosis, indicating that structural compromise is central to the disease process [N4-F3]. The evidence also links attachment loss to apical migration of the junctional epithelium, which leads to pocket formation and loss of attachment [N4-F3]. Similarly, bone resorption is a hallmark of advanced periodontitis and is associated with clinical attachment loss and alveolar bone destruction [N4-F3].

Inflammation and infection compromise ligament and epithelial defenses by turning the initial inflammatory response into a destructive process. The evidence states that the initial inflammation in periodontal tissues should be considered a physiologic defense mechanism against microbial challenge, but if the insult is not resolved, the response becomes chronic and pathologic [N3-F2]. In periodontitis, the inflammatory response is not only a consequence of bacterial challenge but also contributes to tissue destruction because the host’s immune response aims to eliminate infection while inadvertently damaging the periodontium [N4-F3]. The same source explains that inflammation results in progressive destruction of periodontal tissues, leading to attachment loss and bone loss [N4-F3]. This means that the ligament and surrounding tissues are no longer able to function as a stable support system, and the epithelial barrier becomes increasingly vulnerable.

Clinically, the consequences of this disruption are mobility, pocket formation, and tooth loss. Periodontitis can lead to tooth mobility, bone loss, bad breath, and eventually tooth loss [N4-R2]. The evidence also notes that tooth mobility parameters in chronic periodontitis patients include maximum clinical attachment loss and linear radiographic bone loss [N4-R4]. Inflammation can further increase tooth mobility even after inflammation resolves, because residual mobility may persist and continue to affect stability [N4-R3]. Pocket formation is directly tied to the loss of junctional epithelium and the migration of biofilm into the pocket, creating an environment for anaerobic bacteria to proliferate [N4-F3]. Tooth loss is the end result when the supportive tissues are destroyed and the tooth can no longer remain anchored in the jaw [N4-R2][N4-F3].

Taken together, periodontal damage disrupts tooth support by removing the anchoring and buffering roles of the periodontium, while infection control is undermined by chronic inflammation, epithelial barrier breakdown, and the inability of the tissues to prevent microbial access to deeper structures [N4-F3][N4-R2][N3-F2].

The periodontium’s structural components physically support teeth through a coordinated system of anchoring, force distribution, and boundary formation. Alveolar bone anchors the tooth in the jaw because the periodontium includes alveolar bone as one of its four main components [N1-F1], and the periodontal ligament connects the tooth’s cementum to the gingivae in the alveolar socket [N1-F1]. The evidence also states that the periodontium functions include supporting the tooth and making the attachment of the tooth to the bone possible [N1-F1]. Clinically, this anchoring is essential because the alveolar bone provides the rigid framework that holds the tooth root in place within the jaw.

The periodontal ligament distributes chewing forces and absorbs shock because it is the most deformable tissue in the periodontium and stress/strain within the PDL is the key to orthodontic tooth movement [N2-R5]. The same evidence base says that remodeling processes of the alveolar support structures are triggered by alterations in stress/strain distribution in the periodontium [N2-R1], and that orthodontic force activates a series of biological reactions that lead to remodeling [N2-R4]. This indicates that the PDL acts as a shock-absorbing cushion, distributing the forces generated during mastication and protecting the tooth and surrounding bone from damage. Its collagen bands and fibroblasts also allow for proprioception, relaying information to the somatosensory cortex to avoid excessive occlusal forces during mastication and speech [N1-F1].

Cementum anchors the ligament and interfaces with the tooth root by serving as the attachment site for the periodontal ligament [N1-F1]. It is described as the mineralized tissue covering the dentin surfaces and as the attachment site for PDL [N1-F1][N5-F4]. The evidence further explains that cementum is an avascular mineralized structure around the tooth that can anchor periodontal ligament fibers to the root surface, thereby connecting teeth to alveolar bone [N5-F4]. Its most important function is to serve as an anchor point for the main PDL fibers on the surface of the tooth root, helping maintain the occlusal relationship and support the teeth through a dynamically responsive system [N5-F4]. This anchoring is essential for maintaining tooth stability and preventing excessive resorption or ankylosis.

Gingival tissue provides the soft tissue boundary around the tooth. The periodontium includes gingival tissue as one of its four components [N1-F1], and the gingival epithelium is composed of stratified squamous epithelium with keratinized and non-keratinized surfaces [N1-F1]. The gingival component is derived from the ectoderm of the pharyngeal arches and contains keratinized stratified squamous epithelium on its masticatory surface and non-keratinized on its crevicular and junctional surface [N1-F1]. This soft-tissue boundary is important because it creates the first barrier against oral microflora and helps maintain the integrity of the periodontal environment [N1-F1]. It also supports the gingival crevicular fluid and junctional epithelium, which are part of the periodontium’s protective architecture [N1-F1].

Overall, the periodontium’s structural components work together to support teeth: alveolar bone provides the anchoring framework, the PDL distributes and absorbs chewing forces, cementum anchors the ligament to the root, and gingival tissue forms the soft-tissue boundary around the tooth [N1-F1][N2-R5][N5-F4]. This integrated system ensures that the tooth remains stable while also buffering against mechanical stress.

The periodontium protects teeth from microbial infection through a combination of structural barriers, gingival crevicular fluid, and immune/inflammatory responses. Gingival crevicular fluid and epithelial barrier functions are central to pathogen exclusion. The evidence notes that the gingival epithelium is composed of stratified squamous epithelium, and the junctional epithelium is the closest to the tooth surface and attaches to it with hemidesmosomes [N1-F1]. It also states that the gingival tissues and gingival crevicular fluid contain a complex array of immune components that not only bathe the gingival sulcus but also participate in host defense [N3-R4]. The same source emphasizes that the gingival epithelium and crevicular fluid harbor pattern recognition receptors that detect microbial molecular patterns and initiate rapid responses [N3-R5]. This means the epithelial barrier is not passive but actively contributes to early microbial exclusion.

Immune and inflammatory responses limit microbial spread by mobilizing defenses against infection. The evidence explicitly states that the initial inflammation in periodontal tissues should be considered a physiologic defense mechanism against microbial challenge rather than pathology [N3-F2]. However, if the insult is not resolved, the response becomes chronic and pathologic, and the adaptive immune response is activated with involvement of cellular and non-cellular mechanisms of acquired immunity [N3-F2]. The same source explains that immune mechanisms play further roles in the resolution of inflammation and in the healing process, including the repair and regeneration of lost or damaged tissues [N3-F2]. In periodontitis, the immune response is described as an attempt to eliminate infection and protect against bacteria, but it inadvertently damages the periodontium, contributing to disease progression [N4-F3]. This dual role means inflammation can both defend against pathogens and, if excessive or unresolved, contribute to tissue destruction.

Structural integrity prevents microbial access to deeper tissues by maintaining the physical boundary between the oral environment and the tooth-supporting structures. The evidence notes that the periodontium includes the gingiva, periodontal ligament, cementum, and alveolar bone [N1-F1], and that the junctional epithelium is the closest to the tooth surface [N1-F1]. When this boundary is intact, the gingival crevicular fluid and epithelium can bathe the sulcus and exclude pathogens [N3-R4]. The evidence also states that the gingival crevicular fluid amount increases in response to an initial insult, attracting polymorphonuclear neutrophils and T lymphocytes [N4-F3]. This indicates that structural integrity supports an early immune response that can limit microbial spread before infection penetrates deeper into the periodontium. When structural integrity is compromised, however, biofilm can migrate into the pocket and create an environment for anaerobic bacteria to proliferate [N4-F3].

In summary, the periodontium protects teeth from microbial infection through a multi-layered defense: the epithelial barrier and gingival crevicular fluid exclude pathogens and provide early immune sensing, immune and inflammatory responses aim to control infection but can become destructive if unresolved, and structural integrity prevents microbes from accessing deeper tissues [N3-R4][N3-F2][N4-F3][N3-R5].

Periodontal tissues repair and regenerate after injury through mechanisms involving cementum, bone, and ligament regeneration, with inflammation, stem cells, and the extracellular matrix playing key roles. The evidence shows that cementum regeneration is essential for fostering the attachment of new fibrous tissues, maintaining the integrity of the PDL, and preventing tooth ankylosis [N5-F4]. It also states that the regeneration of cementum is considered vital for the development of periodontal tissue and is an important step in periodontal regeneration [N5-F4]. Bone regeneration is similarly important, as the evidence notes that guided tissue regeneration (GTR) and bone grafting are effective only for bone regeneration but have yielded limited success in regenerating the structural and functional aspects of cementum [N5-F4]. This suggests that regeneration is not just about replacing one tissue but restoring the complex multitissue periodontal complex.

Cementum, bone, and ligament regeneration are supported by inflammation, stem cells, and the extracellular matrix. The evidence states that inflammation is part of the healing process and that immune mechanisms play roles in resolution of inflammation and in the repair and regeneration of lost or damaged tissues [N3-F2]. It also emphasizes that innate (inflammatory) immunity and acquired immunity must be coordinated to return the injured tissue to homeostasis [N3-F2]. In terms of stem cells, the evidence indicates that mesenchymal stem cells can create collagen fibers that form alveolar bone and cementum [N6-R4], and that PDLSCs can differentiate into cells concerned with the synthesis and resorption of alveolar bone and the fibrous connective tissue of the ligament and cementum [N6-R5]. This shows that stem-cell-based therapies are positioned as promising tools for periodontal tissue regeneration.

The extracellular matrix is also central to repair. The evidence notes that the periodontal ligament is a connective tissue consisting mostly of type I collagen bands and fibroblasts, and that fibroblasts are involved in forming and repairing alveolar bone and cementum [N1-F1]. The regeneration literature further emphasizes that understanding how cementum regenerates lags behind knowledge of other periodontal tissues and that cementogenic procedures for PDL attachments remain a challenge in periodontal regeneration [N5-F4]. This highlights the importance of the extracellular matrix in supporting tissue reorganization and functional recovery.

Repair can restore both support and infection control. The evidence states that regeneration of cementum is essential for fostering attachment of new fibrous tissues and maintaining PDL integrity [N5-F4], which directly supports tooth stability. It also notes that the regeneration of cementum, especially when it incorporates functional fibres, is vital for the development of periodontal tissue [N5-F4]. In terms of infection control, the evidence links inflammation and immune responses to the resolution of infection and tissue repair, while structural regeneration restores the physical barriers that prevent microbial access [N3-F2][N4-F3]. The clinical context provided by the pathophysiology evidence further supports this by showing that restoration of periodontal tissue is needed because traditional treatments such as scaling and root planing delay inflammation but cannot restore the original connective tissue and reconstruct the intricate organisation of the periodontal complex [N5-F4].

Overall, periodontal tissues repair and regenerate after injury through a coordinated process involving cementum, bone, and ligament regeneration, with inflammation, stem cells, and the extracellular matrix driving the healing response. Repair can restore support by rebuilding the anchoring and buffering structures of the periodontium and can restore infection control by re-establishing barriers and immune defenses [N5-F4][N6-R4][N6-R5][N3-F2].

## How the periodontium’s structural components work together to support and protect teeth

The periodontium is a highly integrated system that supports teeth physically and protects them from damage and microbial infection. It consists of four main components: **alveolar bone**, **periodontal ligament (PDL)**, **cementum**, and **gingival tissue** [N1-F1]. These tissues do not function in isolation; rather, they interact in a coordinated way to anchor the tooth, distribute forces, create a barrier against infection, and respond to injury. The evidence shows that this system can be disrupted by periodontal disease, which weakens tooth support and compromises infection control, and that repair depends on regeneration of cementum, bone, and ligament alongside inflammation, stem cells, and the extracellular matrix [N1-F1][N3-F2][N5-F4][N4-F3].

---

## 1) Structural support: anchoring, force distribution, and boundary formation

### Alveolar bone anchors the tooth in the jaw
Alveolar bone provides the rigid framework that holds the tooth root in place within the jaw [N1-F1]. It is the anchoring component of the periodontium, and its destruction is a central feature of periodontitis [N4-F3]. Without intact alveolar bone, the tooth loses its stable foundation, which is why attachment loss and bone resorption are key indicators of disease progression [N4-F3].

### Periodontal ligament distributes chewing forces and absorbs shock
The periodontal ligament is the most deformable tissue in the periodontium and plays a central biomechanical role [N2-R5]. Stress/strain within the PDL is the key to orthodontic tooth movement, and remodeling of the alveolar support structures is triggered by changes in stress/strain distribution in the periodontium [N2-R1][N2-R4]. This means the PDL acts as a shock absorber and force distributor, protecting the tooth and surrounding bone from excessive mechanical stress during chewing and speech [N2-R5]. It also relays information to the somatosensory cortex through proprioception, helping the body avoid excessive occlusal forces [N1-F1].

### Cementum anchors the ligament and interfaces with the tooth root
Cementum is the mineralized tissue that covers the dentin surfaces and serves as the attachment site for the periodontal ligament [N1-F1][N5-F4]. It anchors the PDL fibers to the root surface, thereby connecting teeth to alveolar bone [N5-F4]. Its most important function is to serve as an anchor point for the main PDL fibers on the surface of the tooth root, helping maintain the occlusal relationship and support the teeth through a dynamically responsive system [N5-F4]. This anchoring is essential for maintaining tooth stability and preventing excessive resorption or ankylosis [N5-F4].

### Gingival tissue provides the soft tissue boundary around the tooth
The gingival component of the periodontium is derived from the ectoderm of the pharyngeal arches and contains keratinized stratified squamous epithelium on its masticatory surface and non-keratinized on its crevicular and junctional surface [N1-F1]. This soft-tissue boundary forms the first barrier against oral microflora and helps maintain the integrity of the periodontal environment [N1-F1]. The junctional epithelium is the closest to the tooth surface and attaches to it with hemidesmosomes [N1-F1], reinforcing the physical boundary that separates the oral cavity from deeper periodontal structures.

---

## 2) Protection against microbial infection

### Structural barriers and gingival crevicular fluid exclude pathogens
The periodontium protects teeth from microbial infection through a combination of structural barriers and gingival crevicular fluid. The gingival epithelium and crevicular fluid contain a complex array of immune components that not only bathe the gingival sulcus but also participate in host defense [N3-R4]. The gingival epithelium and crevicular fluid also harbor pattern recognition receptors that detect microbial molecular patterns and initiate rapid responses [N3-R5]. This means the epithelial barrier is not passive but actively contributes to early microbial exclusion.

### Immune and inflammatory responses limit microbial spread
The initial inflammation in periodontal tissues should be considered a physiologic defense mechanism against microbial challenge rather than pathology [N3-F2]. However, if the insult is not resolved, the response becomes chronic and pathologic, and the adaptive immune response is activated with involvement of cellular and non-cellular mechanisms of acquired immunity [N3-F2]. Immune mechanisms also play further roles in the resolution of inflammation and in the healing process, including the repair and regeneration of lost or damaged tissues [N3-F2]. In periodontitis, the immune response aims to eliminate infection and protect against bacteria, but it inadvertently damages the periodontium, contributing to disease progression [N4-F3]. This dual role means that inflammation can both defend against pathogens and, if excessive or unresolved, contribute to tissue destruction.

### Structural integrity prevents microbial access to deeper tissues
Structural integrity is essential for preventing microbial access to deeper tissues. The periodontium includes the gingiva, periodontal ligament, cementum, and alveolar bone [N1-F1], and the junctional epithelium is the closest to the tooth surface [N1-F1]. When this boundary is intact, the gingival crevicular fluid and epithelium can bathe the sulcus and exclude pathogens [N3-R4]. The evidence also states that the gingival crevicular fluid amount increases in response to an initial insult, attracting polymorphonuclear neutrophils and T lymphocytes [N4-F3]. This indicates that structural integrity supports an early immune response that can limit microbial spread before infection penetrates deeper into the periodontium. When structural integrity is compromised, biofilm can migrate into the pocket and create an environment for anaerobic bacteria to proliferate [N4-F3].

---

## 3) What happens when periodontal damage disrupts support and infection control

### Attachment loss and bone resorption weaken tooth stability
Periodontitis causes progressive destruction of the periodontal tissues, with loss of attachment, alveolar bone resorption, and eventual tooth loss [N4-F3]. Clinical signs such as gingival bleeding, periodontal pocketing, radiographic bone loss, and tooth mobility are used for diagnosis [N4-F3]. Attachment loss is directly linked to apical migration of the junctional epithelium, which leads to pocket formation and loss of attachment [N4-F3]. Bone resorption is a hallmark of advanced periodontitis and is associated with clinical attachment loss and alveolar bone destruction [N4-F3].

### Inflammation and infection compromise ligament and epithelial defenses
Inflammation and infection compromise the ligament and epithelial defenses by turning the initial inflammatory response into a destructive process. The evidence states that the initial inflammation in periodontal tissues is a physiologic defense mechanism against microbial challenge, but if the insult is not resolved, the response becomes chronic and pathologic [N3-F2]. In periodontitis, the inflammatory response is not only a consequence of bacterial challenge but also contributes to tissue destruction because the host’s immune response aims to eliminate infection while inadvertently damaging the periodontium [N4-F3]. This means that the ligament and surrounding tissues are no longer able to function as a stable support system, and the epithelial barrier becomes increasingly vulnerable.

### Clinical consequences such as mobility, pocket formation, and tooth loss
Clinically, the consequences of this disruption are mobility, pocket formation, and tooth loss. Periodontitis can lead to tooth mobility, bone loss, bad breath, and eventually tooth loss [N4-R2]. The evidence also notes that tooth mobility parameters in chronic periodontitis patients include maximum clinical attachment loss and linear radiographic bone loss [N4-R4]. Inflammation can further increase tooth mobility even after inflammation resolves, because residual mobility may persist and continue to affect stability [N4-R3]. Pocket formation is directly tied to the loss of junctional epithelium and the migration of biofilm into the pocket, creating an environment for anaerobic bacteria to proliferate [N4-F3]. Tooth loss is the end result when the supportive tissues are destroyed and the tooth can no longer remain anchored in the jaw [N4-R2][N4-F3].

---

## 4) Repair and regeneration after injury

### Mechanisms of cementum, bone, and ligament regeneration
Periodontal tissues repair and regenerate after injury through mechanisms involving cementum, bone, and ligament regeneration. The evidence shows that cementum regeneration is essential for fostering the attachment of new fibrous tissues, maintaining the integrity of the PDL, and preventing tooth ankylosis [N5-F4]. It also states that regeneration of cementum is considered vital for the development of periodontal tissue and is an important step in periodontal regeneration [N5-F4]. Bone regeneration is similarly important, but traditional treatments such as scaling and root planing can delay inflammation but cannot restore the original connective tissue or reconstruct the intricate organisation of the periodontal complex [N5-F4]. This means regeneration is not just about replacing one tissue but restoring the complex multitissue periodontal complex.

### Roles of inflammation, stem cells, and the extracellular matrix in repair
Inflammation, stem cells, and the extracellular matrix all play key roles in repair. The evidence states that inflammation is part of the healing process and that immune mechanisms play roles in resolution of inflammation and in the repair and regeneration of lost or damaged tissues [N3-F2]. Innate (inflammatory) immunity and acquired immunity must be coordinated to return the injured tissue to homeostasis [N3-F2]. In terms of stem cells, the evidence indicates that mesenchymal stem cells can create collagen fibers that form alveolar bone and cementum [N6-R4], and that PDLSCs can differentiate into cells concerned with the synthesis and resorption of alveolar bone and the fibrous connective tissue of the ligament and cementum [N6-R5]. This shows that stem-cell-based therapies are positioned as promising tools for periodontal tissue regeneration. The extracellular matrix is also central to repair, as the periodontal ligament is a connective tissue consisting mostly of type I collagen bands and fibroblasts, and fibroblasts are involved in forming and repairing alveolar bone and cementum [N1-F1].

### How repair can restore support and infection control
Repair can restore both support and infection control. The evidence states that regeneration of cementum is essential for fostering attachment of new fibrous tissues and maintaining PDL integrity [N5-F4], which directly supports tooth stability. It also notes that regeneration of cementum, especially when it incorporates functional fibers, is vital for the development of periodontal tissue [N5-F4]. In terms of infection control, the evidence links inflammation and immune responses to the resolution of infection and tissue repair, while structural regeneration restores the physical barriers that prevent microbial access [N3-F2][N4-F3]. This means that successful repair not only rebuilds the anchoring and buffering structures of the periodontium but also re-establishes the defenses that protect against microbial infection.

---

## Conclusion

The periodontium supports and protects teeth through a coordinated system of anchoring, force distribution, boundary formation, and immune defense. Alveolar bone anchors the tooth, the periodontal ligament distributes and absorbs chewing forces, cementum anchors the ligament to the root, and gingival tissue forms the soft-tissue boundary around the tooth [N1-F1][N2-R5][N5-F4]. At the same time, the periodontium protects teeth from microbial infection through structural barriers, gingival crevicular fluid, and immune/inflammatory responses [N3-R4][N3-F2][N4-F3]. When periodontal damage occurs, attachment loss, bone resorption, inflammation, and infection weaken tooth support and compromise defenses [N4-F3][N4-R2]. However, repair and regeneration can restore support and infection control by rebuilding cementum, bone, and ligament, with inflammation, stem cells, and the extracellular matrix driving the healing response [N5-F4][N6-R4][N6-R5][N3-F2]. Overall, the periodontium functions as an integrated biological system that keeps teeth stable, resilient, and protected.

## How the periodontium’s structural components work together to support and protect teeth

The periodontium is a highly integrated system that supports teeth physically and protects them from damage and microbial infection. It consists of four main components: **alveolar bone**, **periodontal ligament (PDL)**, **cementum**, and **gingival tissue** [N1-F1]. These tissues do not function in isolation; rather, they interact in a coordinated way to anchor the tooth, distribute forces, create a barrier against infection, and respond to injury. The evidence shows that this system can be disrupted by periodontal disease, which weakens tooth support and compromises infection control, and that repair depends on regeneration of cementum, bone, and ligament alongside inflammation, stem cells, and the extracellular matrix [N1-F1][N3-F2][N5-F4][N4-F3].

---

## 1) Structural support: anchoring, force distribution, and boundary formation

### Alveolar bone anchors the tooth in the jaw
Alveolar bone provides the rigid framework that holds the tooth root in place within the jaw [N1-F1]. It is the anchoring component of the periodontium, and its destruction is a central feature of periodontitis [N4-F3]. Without intact alveolar bone, the tooth loses its stable foundation, which is why attachment loss and bone resorption are key indicators of disease progression [N4-F3].

### Periodontal ligament distributes chewing forces and absorbs shock
The periodontal ligament is the most deformable tissue in the periodontium and plays a central biomechanical role [N2-R5]. Stress/strain within the PDL is the key to orthodontic tooth movement, and remodeling of the alveolar support structures is triggered by changes in stress/strain distribution in the periodontium [N2-R1][N2-R4]. This means the PDL acts as a shock absorber and force distributor, protecting the tooth and surrounding bone from excessive mechanical stress during chewing and speech [N2-R5]. It also relays information to the somatosensory cortex through proprioception, helping the body avoid excessive occlusal forces [N1-F1].

### Cementum anchors the ligament and interfaces with the tooth root
Cementum is the mineralized tissue that covers the dentin surfaces and serves as the attachment site for the periodontal ligament [N1-F1][N5-F4]. It anchors the PDL fibers to the root surface, thereby connecting teeth to alveolar bone [N5-F4]. Its most important function is to serve as an anchor point for the main PDL fibers on the surface of the tooth root, helping maintain the occlusal relationship and support the teeth through a dynamically responsive system [N5-F4]. This anchoring is essential for maintaining tooth stability and preventing excessive resorption or ankylosis [N5-F4].

### Gingival tissue provides the soft tissue boundary around the tooth
The gingival component of the periodontium is derived from the ectoderm of the pharyngeal arches and contains keratinized stratified squamous epithelium on its masticatory surface and non-keratinized on its crevicular and junctional surface [N1-F1]. This soft-tissue boundary forms the first barrier against oral microflora and helps maintain the integrity of the periodontal environment [N1-F1]. The junctional epithelium is the closest to the tooth surface and attaches to it with hemidesmosomes [N1-F1], reinforcing the physical boundary that separates the oral cavity from deeper periodontal structures.

## 2) Protection against microbial infection

### Structural barriers and gingival crevicular fluid exclude pathogens
The periodontium protects teeth from microbial infection through a combination of structural barriers and gingival crevicular fluid. The gingival epithelium and crevicular fluid contain a complex array of immune components that not only bathe the gingival sulcus but also participate in host defense [N3-R4]. The gingival epithelium and crevicular fluid also harbor pattern recognition receptors that detect microbial molecular patterns and initiate rapid responses [N3-R5]. This means the epithelial barrier is not passive but actively contributes to early microbial exclusion.

### Immune and inflammatory responses limit microbial spread
The initial inflammation in periodontal tissues should be considered a physiologic defense mechanism against microbial challenge rather than pathology [N3-F2]. However, if the insult is not resolved, the response becomes chronic and pathologic, and the adaptive immune response is activated with involvement of cellular and non-cellular mechanisms of acquired immunity [N3-F2]. Immune mechanisms also play further roles in the resolution of inflammation and in the healing process, including the repair and regeneration of lost or damaged tissues [N3-F2]. In periodontitis, the immune response aims to eliminate infection and protect against bacteria, but it inadvertently damages the periodontium, contributing to disease progression [N4-F3]. This dual role means that inflammation can both defend against pathogens and, if excessive or unresolved, contribute to tissue destruction.

### Structural integrity prevents microbial access to deeper tissues
Structural integrity is essential for preventing microbial access to deeper tissues. The periodontium includes the gingiva, periodontal ligament, cementum, and alveolar bone [N1-F1], and the junctional epithelium is the closest to the tooth surface [N1-F1]. When this boundary is intact, the gingival crevicular fluid and epithelium can bathe the sulcus and exclude pathogens [N3-R4]. The evidence also states that the gingival crevicular fluid amount increases in response to an initial insult, attracting polymorphonuclear neutrophils and T lymphocytes [N4-F3]. This indicates that structural integrity supports an early immune response that can limit microbial spread before infection penetrates deeper into the periodontium. When structural integrity is compromised, biofilm can migrate into the pocket and create an environment for anaerobic bacteria to proliferate [N4-F3].

---

## 3) What happens when periodontal damage disrupts support and infection control

### Attachment loss and bone resorption weaken tooth stability
Periodontitis causes progressive destruction of the periodontal tissues, with loss of attachment, alveolar bone resorption, and eventual tooth loss [N4-F3]. Clinical signs such as gingival bleeding, periodontal pocketing, radiographic bone loss, and tooth mobility are used for diagnosis [N4-F3]. Attachment loss is directly linked to apical migration of the junctional epithelium, which leads to pocket formation and loss of attachment [N4-F3]. Bone resorption is a hallmark of advanced periodontitis and is associated with clinical attachment loss and alveolar bone destruction [N4-F3].

### Inflammation and infection compromise ligament and epithelial defenses
Inflammation and infection compromise the ligament and epithelial defenses by turning the initial inflammatory response into a destructive process. The evidence states that the initial inflammation in periodontal tissues is a physiologic defense mechanism against microbial challenge, but if the insult is not resolved, the response becomes chronic and pathologic [N3-F2]. In periodontitis, the inflammatory response is not only a consequence of bacterial challenge but also contributes to tissue destruction because the host’s immune response aims to eliminate infection while inadvertently damaging the periodontium [N4-F3]. This means that the ligament and surrounding tissues are no longer able to function as a stable support system, and the epithelial barrier becomes increasingly vulnerable.

Clinically, the consequences of this disruption are mobility, pocket formation, and tooth loss. Periodontitis can lead to tooth mobility, bone loss, bad breath, and eventually tooth loss [N4-R2]. The evidence also notes that tooth mobility parameters in chronic periodontitis patients include maximum clinical attachment loss and linear radiographic bone loss [N4-R4]. Inflammation can further increase tooth mobility even after inflammation resolves, because residual mobility may persist and continue to affect stability [N4-R3]. Pocket formation is directly tied to the loss of junctional epithelium and the migration of biofilm into the pocket, creating an environment for anaerobic bacteria to proliferate [N4-F3]. ## 4) Repair and regeneration after injury

### Mechanisms of cementum, bone, and ligament regeneration
Periodontal tissues repair and regenerate after injury through mechanisms involving cementum, bone, and ligament regeneration. The evidence shows that cementum regeneration is essential for fostering the attachment of new fibrous tissues, maintaining the integrity of the PDL, and preventing tooth ankylosis [N5-F4]. It also states that regeneration of cementum is considered vital for the development of periodontal tissue and is an important step in periodontal regeneration [N5-F4]. This means regeneration is not just about replacing one tissue but restoring the complex multitissue periodontal complex.

### Roles of inflammation, stem cells, and the extracellular matrix in repair
Inflammation, stem cells, and the extracellular matrix all play key roles in repair. The evidence states that inflammation is part of the healing process and that immune mechanisms play roles in resolution of inflammation and in the repair and regeneration of lost or damaged tissues [N3-F2]. Innate (inflammatory) immunity and acquired immunity must be coordinated to return the injured tissue to homeostasis [N3-F2]. The extracellular matrix is also central to repair, as the periodontal ligament is a connective tissue consisting mostly of type I collagen bands and fibroblasts, and fibroblasts are involved in forming and repairing alveolar bone and cementum [N1-F1].

### How repair can restore support and infection control
Repair can restore both support and infection control. The evidence states that regeneration of cementum is essential for fostering attachment of new fibrous tissues and maintaining PDL integrity [N5-F4], which directly supports tooth stability. It also notes that regeneration of cementum, especially when it incorporates functional fibers, is vital for the development of periodontal tissue [N5-F4]. In terms of infection control, the evidence links inflammation and immune responses to the resolution of infection and tissue repair, while structural regeneration restores the physical barriers that prevent microbial access [N3-F2][N4-F3]. This means that successful repair not only rebuilds the anchoring and buffering structures of the periodontium but also re-establishes the defenses that protect against microbial infection.

---

## Conclusion

The periodontium supports and protects teeth through a coordinated system of anchoring, force distribution, boundary formation, and immune defense. Alveolar bone anchors the tooth, the periodontal ligament distributes and absorbs chewing forces, cementum anchors the ligament to the root, and gingival tissue forms the soft-tissue boundary around the tooth [N1-F1][N2-R5][N5-F4]. At the same time, the periodontium protects teeth from microbial infection through structural barriers, gingival crevicular fluid, and immune/inflammatory responses [N3-R4][N3-F2][N4-F3]. When periodontal damage occurs, attachment loss, bone resorption, inflammation, and infection weaken tooth support and compromise defenses [N4-F3][N4-R2]. However, repair and regeneration can restore support and infection control by rebuilding cementum, bone, and ligament, with inflammation, stem cells, and the extracellular matrix driving the healing response [N5-F4][N6-R4][N6-R5][N3-F2]. Overall, the periodontium functions as an integrated biological system that keeps teeth stable, resilient, and protected.

It consists of four main components: **alveolar bone**, **periodontal ligament (PDL)**, **cementum**, and **gingival tissue** [N1-F1]. ## 1) Structural support: anchoring, force distribution, and boundary formation

### Alveolar bone anchors the tooth in the jaw
Alveolar bone provides the rigid framework that holds the tooth root in place within the jaw [N1-F1]. It is the anchoring component of the periodontium, and its destruction is a central feature of periodontitis [N4-F3]. Without intact alveolar bone, the tooth loses its stable foundation, which is why attachment loss and bone resorption are key indicators of disease progression [N4-F3].

### Periodontal ligament distributes chewing forces and absorbs shock
The periodontal ligament is the most deformable tissue in the periodontium and plays a central biomechanical role [N2-R5]. Stress/strain within the PDL is the key to orthodontic tooth movement, and remodeling of the alveolar support structures is triggered by changes in stress/strain distribution in the periodontium [N2-R1][N2-R4]. This means the PDL acts as a shock absorber and force distributor, protecting the tooth and surrounding bone from excessive mechanical stress during chewing and speech [N2-R5]. It also relays information to the somatosensory cortex through proprioception, helping the body avoid excessive occlusal forces [N1-F1].

### Cementum anchors the ligament and interfaces with the tooth root
Cementum is the mineralized tissue that covers the dentin surfaces and serves as the attachment site for the periodontal ligament [N1-F1][N5-F4]. It anchors the PDL fibers to the root surface, thereby connecting teeth to alveolar bone [N5-F4]. Its most important function is to serve as an anchor point for the main PDL fibers on the surface of the tooth root, helping maintain the occlusal relationship and support the teeth through a dynamically responsive system [N5-F4]. This anchoring is essential for maintaining tooth stability and preventing excessive resorption or ankylosis [N5-F4].

### Gingival tissue provides the soft tissue boundary around the tooth
The gingival component of the periodontium is derived from the ectoderm of the pharyngeal arches and contains keratinized stratified squamous epithelium on its masticatory surface and non-keratinized on its crevicular and junctional surface [N1-F1]. This soft-tissue boundary forms the first barrier against oral microflora and helps maintain the integrity of the periodontal environment [N1-F1]. The junctional epithelium is the closest to the tooth surface and attaches to it with hemidesmosomes [N1-F1], reinforcing the physical boundary that separates the oral cavity from deeper periodontal structures.

---

## 2) Protection against microbial infection

### Structural barriers and gingival crevicular fluid exclude pathogens
The periodontium protects teeth from microbial infection through a combination of structural barriers and gingival crevicular fluid. The gingival epithelium and crevicular fluid contain a complex array of immune components that not only bathe the gingival sulcus but also participate in host defense [N3-R4]. The gingival epithelium and crevicular fluid also harbor pattern recognition receptors that detect microbial molecular patterns and initiate rapid responses [N3-R5]. This means the epithelial barrier is not passive but actively contributes to early microbial exclusion.

The initial inflammation in periodontal tissues should be considered a physiologic defense mechanism against microbial challenge rather than pathology [N3-F2]. However, if the insult is not resolved, the response becomes chronic and pathologic, and the adaptive immune response is activated with involvement of cellular and non-cellular mechanisms of acquired immunity [N3-F2]. Immune mechanisms also play further roles in the resolution of inflammation and in the healing process, including the repair and regeneration of lost or damaged tissues [N3-F2]. In periodontitis, the immune response aims to eliminate infection and protect against bacteria, but it inadvertently damages the periodontium, contributing to disease progression [N4-F3]. This dual role means that inflammation can both defend against pathogens and, if excessive or unresolved, contribute to tissue destruction.

### Structural integrity prevents microbial access to deeper tissues
Structural integrity is essential for preventing microbial access to deeper tissues. The periodontium includes the gingiva, periodontal ligament, cementum, and alveolar bone [N1-F1], and the junctional epithelium is the closest to the tooth surface [N1-F1]. When this boundary is intact, the gingival crevicular fluid and epithelium can bathe the sulcus and exclude pathogens [N3-R4]. The evidence also states that the gingival crevicular fluid amount increases in response to an initial insult, attracting polymorphonuclear neutrophils and T lymphocytes [N4-F3]. This indicates that structural integrity supports an early immune response that can limit microbial spread before infection penetrates deeper into the periodontium. When structural integrity is compromised, biofilm can migrate into the pocket and create an environment for anaerobic bacteria to proliferate [N4-F3].

---

### Attachment loss and bone resorption weaken tooth stability
Periodontitis causes progressive destruction of the periodontal tissues, with loss of attachment, alveolar bone resorption, and eventual tooth loss [N4-F3]. Clinical signs such as gingival bleeding, periodontal pocketing, radiographic bone loss, and tooth mobility are used for diagnosis [N4-F3]. Attachment loss is directly linked to apical migration of the junctional epithelium, which leads to pocket formation and loss of attachment [N4-F3]. Bone resorption is a hallmark of advanced periodontitis and is associated with clinical attachment loss and alveolar bone destruction [N4-F3].

Inflammation and infection compromise the ligament and epithelial defenses by turning the initial inflammatory response into a destructive process. The evidence states that the initial inflammation in periodontal tissues is a physiologic defense mechanism against microbial challenge, but if the insult is not resolved, the response becomes chronic and pathologic [N3-F2]. In periodontitis, the inflammatory response is not only a consequence of bacterial challenge but also contributes to tissue destruction because the host’s immune response aims to eliminate infection while inadvertently damaging the periodontium [N4-F3]. This means that the ligament and surrounding tissues are no longer able to function as a stable support system, and the epithelial barrier becomes increasingly vulnerable.

Clinically, the consequences of this disruption are mobility, pocket formation, and tooth loss. Periodontitis can lead to tooth mobility, bone loss, bad breath, and eventually tooth loss [N4-R2]. The evidence also notes that tooth mobility parameters in chronic periodontitis patients include maximum clinical attachment loss and linear radiographic bone loss [N4-R4]. Inflammation can further increase tooth mobility even after inflammation resolves, because residual mobility may persist and continue to affect stability [N4-R3]. Pocket formation is directly tied to the loss of junctional epithelium and the migration of biofilm into the pocket, creating an environment for anaerobic bacteria to proliferate [N4-F3]. Tooth loss is the end result when the supportive tissues are destroyed and the tooth can no longer remain anchored in the jaw [N4-R2][N4-F3].

### Mechanisms of cementum, bone, and ligament regeneration
Periodontal tissues repair and regenerate after injury through mechanisms involving cementum, bone, and ligament regeneration. The evidence shows that cementum regeneration is essential for fostering the attachment of new fibrous tissues, maintaining the integrity of the PDL, and preventing tooth ankylosis [N5-F4]. This means regeneration is not just about replacing one tissue but restoring the complex multitissue periodontal complex.

Inflammation, stem cells, and the extracellular matrix all play key roles in repair. The evidence states that inflammation is part of the healing process and that immune mechanisms play roles in resolution of inflammation and in the repair and regeneration of lost or damaged tissues [N3-F2]. Innate (inflammatory) immunity and acquired immunity must be coordinated to return the injured tissue to homeostasis [N3-F2]. In terms of stem cells, the evidence indicates that mesenchymal stem cells can create collagen fibers that form alveolar bone and cementum [N6-R4], and that PDLSCs can differentiate into cells concerned with the synthesis and resorption of alveolar bone and the fibrous connective tissue of the ligament and cementum [N6-R5]. This shows that stem-cell-based therapies are positioned as promising tools for periodontal tissue regeneration. The extracellular matrix is also central to repair, as the periodontal ligament is a connective tissue consisting mostly of type I collagen bands and fibroblasts, and fibroblasts are involved in forming and repairing alveolar bone and cementum [N1-F1].

### How repair can restore support and infection control
Repair can restore both support and infection control. The evidence states that regeneration of cementum is essential for fostering attachment of new fibrous tissues and maintaining PDL integrity [N5-F4], which directly supports tooth stability. It also notes that regeneration of cementum, especially when it incorporates functional fibers, is vital for the development of periodontal tissue [N5-F4]. In terms of infection control, the evidence links inflammation and immune responses to the resolution of infection and tissue repair, while structural regeneration restores the physical barriers that prevent microbial access [N3-F2][N4-F3]. This means that successful repair not only rebuilds the anchoring and buffering structures of the periodontium but also re-establishes the defenses that protect against microbial infection.

---

## Conclusion

The periodontium supports and protects teeth through a coordinated system of anchoring, force distribution, boundary formation, and immune defense. Alveolar bone anchors the tooth, the periodontal ligament distributes and absorbs chewing forces, cementum anchors the ligament to the root, and gingival tissue forms the soft-tissue boundary around the tooth [N1-F1][N2-R5][N5-F4]. At the same time, the periodontium protects teeth from microbial infection through structural barriers, gingival crevicular fluid, and immune/inflammatory responses [N3-R4][N3-F2][N4-F3]. When periodontal damage occurs, attachment loss, bone resorption, inflammation, and infection weaken tooth support and compromise defenses [N4-F3][N4-R2]. However, repair and regeneration can restore support and infection control by rebuilding cementum, bone, and ligament, with inflammation, stem cells, and the extracellular matrix driving the healing response [N5-F4][N6-R4][N6-R5][N3-F2]. Overall, the periodontium functions as an integrated biological system that keeps teeth stable, resilient, and protected.

### Mechanisms of cementum, bone, and ligament regeneration
Periodontal tissues repair and regenerate after injury through mechanisms involving cementum, bone, and ligament regeneration. The evidence shows that cementum regeneration is essential for fostering the attachment of new fibrous tissues, maintaining the integrity of the PDL, and preventing tooth ankylosis [N5-F4]. It also states that regeneration of cementum is considered vital for the development of periodontal tissue and is an important step in periodontal regeneration [N5-F4]. Bone regeneration is similarly important, but traditional treatments such as scaling and root planing can delay inflammation but cannot restore the original connective tissue or reconstruct the intricate organisation of the periodontal complex [N5-F4]. This means regeneration is not just about replacing one tissue but restoring the complex multitissue periodontal complex.

### Roles of inflammation, stem cells, and the extracellular matrix in repair
Inflammation, stem cells, and the extracellular matrix all play key roles in repair. The evidence states that inflammation is part of the healing process and that immune mechanisms play roles in resolution of inflammation and in the repair and regeneration of lost or damaged tissues [N3-F2]. Innate (inflammatory) immunity and acquired immunity must be coordinated to return the injured tissue to homeostasis [N3-F2]. In terms of stem cells, the evidence indicates that mesenchymal stem cells can create collagen fibers that form alveolar bone and cementum [N6-R4], and that PDLSCs can differentiate into cells concerned with the synthesis and resorption of alveolar bone and the fibrous connective tissue of the ligament and cementum [N6-R5]. This shows that stem-cell-based therapies are positioned as promising tools for periodontal tissue regeneration. The extracellular matrix is also central to repair, as the periodontal ligament is a connective tissue consisting mostly of type I collagen bands and fibroblasts, and fibroblasts are involved in forming and repairing alveolar bone and cementum [N1-F1].

### How repair can restore support and infection control
Repair can restore both support and infection control. The evidence states that regeneration of cementum is essential for fostering attachment of new fibrous tissues and maintaining PDL integrity [N5-F4], which directly supports tooth stability. It also notes that regeneration of cementum, especially when it incorporates functional fibers, is vital for the development of periodontal tissue [N5-F4]. In terms of infection control, the evidence links inflammation and immune responses to the resolution of infection and tissue repair, while structural regeneration restores the physical barriers that prevent microbial access [N3-F2][N4-F3]. This means that successful repair not only rebuilds the anchoring and buffering structures of the periodontium but also re-establishes the defenses that protect against microbial infection.

## Conclusion

The periodontium supports and protects teeth through a coordinated system of anchoring, force distribution, boundary formation, and immune defense. Alveolar bone anchors the tooth, the periodontal ligament distributes and absorbs chewing forces, cementum anchors the ligament to the root, and gingival tissue forms the soft-tissue boundary around the tooth [N1-F1][N2-R5][N5-F4]. At the same time, the periodontium protects teeth from microbial infection through structural barriers, gingival crevicular fluid, and immune/inflammatory responses [N3-R4][N3-F2][N4-F3]. When periodontal damage occurs, attachment loss, bone resorption, inflammation, and infection weaken tooth support and compromise defenses [N4-F3][N4-R2]. However, repair and regeneration can restore support and infection control by rebuilding cementum, bone, and ligament, with inflammation, stem cells, and the extracellular matrix driving the healing response [N5-F4][N6-R4][N6-R5][N3-F2]. Overall, the periodontium functions as an integrated biological system that keeps teeth stable, resilient, and protected.
